summary: Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer hosted a second AI Insight Forum on Tuesday with tech leaders, advocates and labor figures, focused on balancing transformational and sustainable AI innovation and on funding it federally. Alongside the forum, Senators Schatz and Kennedy introduced an AI labeling bill, and the Artificial Intelligence Advancement Act of 2023 was already pending. Workers, unions and AI employees pressed for protections while Andreessen and Tegmark represented opposing views on AI pace.
one_line: Schumer's second AI Insight Forum discussed federal AI investment and sustainable innovation as senators introduced an AI content labeling bill and labor groups demanded worker protections.
key_facts: Senator Charles Schumer (D-NY) hosted the second AI Insight Forum on Tuesday, with guests including Marc Andreessen, John Doerr, Max Tegmark of the Future of Life Institute and NAACP CEO Derrick Johnson.
Schumer said "American leadership on AI can't be done on the cheap" and that almost all experts called for robust, sustained federal investment in private and public sectors.
National Security AI Commission estimates put the cost of that investment at around $32 billion a year.
Schumer suggested addressing funding by leveraging the private sector with new mechanisms like the Grand Challenges prize idea.
Senators Brian Schatz (D-HI) and John Kennedy (R-LA) introduced the Schatz-Kennedy AI Labeling Act, requiring generative AI developers to clearly and conspicuously disclose AI-generated content.

The AI Labeling Act would require developers and licensees to take "reasonable steps" to prevent "systematic publication of content without disclosures" and create a working group on non-binding technical standards for social media platforms to identify such content.
The Artificial Intelligence Advancement Act of 2023 (S. 3050) was co-sponsored by Senators Martin Heinrich, Mike Rounds, Charles Schumer and Todd Young.

S. 3050 proposes AI bug bounty programs, a vulnerability analysis study for AI-enabled military applications, a report on AI regulation in financial services, and a report on data sharing and coordination.
SEC Chairman Gary Gensler told The Financial Times that AI regulation in finance is "a hard financial stability issue to address" because most regulation targets individual institutions.
AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler said that if workers and unions are not involved in the innovation process, AI will curtail rights, threaten good jobs and undermine democracy.
The forums are part of Schumer's SAFE Innovation Framework, debuted in June, which aims to keep the US from letting the Chinese Communist Party craft AI standards.
On Monday, employees from two dozen leading AI firms published an open letter to Schumer demanding Congress safeguard their livelihoods.
Senator Ed Markey and Representative Pramila Jayapal had the previous month called on AI companies to answer for the working conditions of their data workers.
Schumer said the conversation would continue in more forums and committee hearings toward comprehensive, bipartisan AI legislation.
